content: 1. Due to the presence of small subgroups, the data may exhibit significant heterogeneity. However, we did not downgrade for inconsistency as the majority of point estimates are similar, with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 84%). This heterogeneity could not be explained by the small subgroups. 2. For another analysis, we observed similar findings with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 63%). Again, this heterogeneity could not be attributed to small subgroups and may represent substantial heterogeneity. No downgrading for inconsistency was applied. 3. In a separate analysis, we downgraded once for inconsistency. While some point estimates were similar with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 97%), the heterogeneity could not be explained by small subgroups and may represent considerable heterogeneity. 4. Another analysis also resulted in a single downgrade for inconsistency. Some point estimates were similar with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 83%), but the heterogeneity could not be explained by small subgroups and may represent considerable heterogeneity. 5. In a further analysis, we downgraded once for inconsistency. Some point estimates were similar with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 88%), but the heterogeneity could not be explained by small subgroups and may represent considerable heterogeneity. 6. In another analysis, no downgrading for inconsistency was applied. The majority of point estimates were similar with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 70%), but the heterogeneity could not be explained by small subgroups and may represent substantial heterogeneity. 7. In a different analysis, we downgraded once for inconsistency. Some point estimates were similar with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 82%), but the heterogeneity could not be explained by small subgroups and may represent considerable heterogeneity. 8. For indirectness, we downgraded once as the trial(s) were conducted in a single low-income country. 9. The study by Smeets (2008) was excluded from the meta-analysis as it only provided within-group mean changes and lacked follow-up scores. This study involved 119 participants and was rated as having an overall low risk of bias. Participants underwent combination treatment (active physical treatment with aerobic and core strengthening exercises plus graded activity with problem-solving training) versus graded activity with problem-solving training alone. 10. The study by Tilbrook (2011) was not included in the meta-analysis as it only reported within-group changes and did not provide follow-up scores. It was rated as having an unclear overall risk of bias. 11. For imprecision, we downgraded once due to a low sample size, as the optimal information size (OIS) was not reached. 12. For inconsistency, we did not downgrade in some analyses where point estimates were similar with overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., I² = 50%, I² = 65%). However, in other cases, heterogeneity was substantial (e.g., I² = 80%, I² = 85%) and could not be explained by small subgroups. 13. For indirectness, we did not downgrade in trials conducted in both highand low-income countries. However, we downgraded once for trials conducted in a single low-income or high-income country. 14. For risk of bias, we downgraded twice in cases where most or all trials were rated as having a high overall risk of bias. 15. In some analyses, no downgrading for inconsistency was applied when I² values were low (e.g., I² = 0%, I² = 9%, I² = 26%). 16. In one analysis, we downgraded once for risk of bias as more than 50% of the weight came from trials with an unclear risk of bias. 17. In another analysis, we downgraded once for indirectness as the trial(s) were conducted in a single low-income country. 18. In a separate analysis, we downgraded once for indirectness as the trial(s) were conducted in a single high-income country. 19. For imprecision, we did not downgrade in cases where the OIS was reached and the confidence interval did not cross the null. 20. In one analysis, we downgraded twice for imprecision due to a low sample size, as the OIS was not reached. 21. In some cases, inconsistency was not downgraded, but there were no additional trials available for comparison. 22. For adverse events, most were classified as non-serious and related to increased pain. One yoga participant experienced severe pain, possibly associated with yoga. In the usual care group, one participant died, and another had a severe accident/injury. In another trial (Zadro 2019), no adverse events were reported among 60 older participants. 23. The benefits and harms of exercise in managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults (including older adults aged 60 years and over) were compared with usual care. Trials included 313 participants in total, with outcomes measured using scales such as the Aberdeen Back Pain Scale (0–100) and the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (0–24), where lower values indicated benefit. 24. The study by Raoul (2019) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. 25. The study by Shu (2021) observed the curative effect of massage manipulation combined with core strength training in patients with chronic non-specific low back pain. 26. The study by Ansari (2020) evaluated the effect of aquatic exercise on functional disability, flexibility, and trunk muscle function in postmenopausal women with chronic non-specific low back pain. 27. The study by Heidari (2018) compared the effects of 8 weeks of core stability exercises on a ball versus sling exercises on quality of life and pain in females with non-specific chronic low back pain. 28. The study by Liu (2018) investigated the effects of Tai Chi on event-related potentials in patients with chronic non-specific low back pain. 29. The study by Shariat (2019) assessed the impact of modified exercise and relaxation therapy on chronic lower back pain in office workers. 30. The study by Chhabra (2018) evaluated the use of a smartphone app in the self-management of chronic low back pain. 31. The study by Jinnouchi (2020) examined the effects of brief self-exercise education on managing chronic low back pain in a community-based, randomized, parallel-group pragmatic trial. 32. The study by Kell (2018) explored the response of individuals with chronic non-specific low back pain to three different volumes of periodized musculoskeletal rehabilitation.
